title: The @utility Directive
subtopics: Supporting Tailwind variants for custom utilities
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of the @utility directive.
Apply one appropriate technique to a small Tailwind CSS example.
Verify the expected result and identify a common failure mode.

content.intro: In this lesson, focus on the @utility directive and connect it to the way Tailwind CSS generates and applies utility styles.
content.why_it_matters: The @utility Directive helps a team reuse visual decisions without losing flexibility for real application interfaces.

content_blocks.title: Module 15 learning map
content_blocks.alt_text: Four-step module learning map: When to Write Custom CSS → The @custom-variant Directive → Understanding Preflight and CSS Layers → Designing Custom Utilities and CSS APIs. Lesson pages add code examples and practice.
content_blocks.caption: Learning map for Module 15, from the opening concept to a practical checkpoint.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum highlights: Defining a custom utility; Simple custom declarations; Complex custom utilities; Reusing custom utilities; Supporting Tailwind variants for custom utilities. Treat these as practical decisions rather than a list to memorize: identify the intended behavior, choose the smallest suitable utility or directive, and inspect what the browser receives.

content_blocks.title: Concepts to understand
items: Supporting Tailwind variants for custom utilities

content_blocks.title: Worked example: The @utility Directive
content_blocks.expected_output: A custom content-auto utility is registered and can be combined with supported variants.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with the example, change one decision related to the @utility directive, then compare the outcome. In a Tailwind-enabled project, confirm the generated CSS exists; class strings alone do not make styles available without a configured build.

content_blocks.title: Version and compatibility note
content_blocks.text: This course prioritizes Tailwind CSS v4. Confirm your installed version and use its matching official guide. Snippets using v3 directives or configuration are labelled as legacy and should not be mixed blindly with v4 syntax.

content.task: Complete the linked practical exercise “Custom utility library”. Register one custom utility with @utility, document its purpose, and test a relevant state variant.
task_acceptance_criteria: Demonstrate at least one decision tied to the @utility directive.
Keep the example easy to inspect, with complete utility names.
Test the outcome and document one limitation or environment assumption.
hints: Identify which listed syllabus topic is most important to the @utility directive.
Change one utility, token, variant or configuration setting at a time.
Inspect generated CSS and computed styles before changing unrelated code.
content.expected_output: A custom content-auto utility is registered and can be combined with supported variants.
troubleshooting: If no style appears, verify the package, CSS import and build-tool integration before changing the HTML.
If only a state or breakpoint style fails, check the full class token, source detection, condition and computed CSS.
For a framework snippet, import the stylesheet through its supported entry point and consult the current official guide.
common_mistakes: Applying the @utility directive without checking generated styles or browser behavior.
Mixing Tailwind v3 and v4 setup examples without a migration plan.
Treating visual appearance as a substitute for semantic markup, keyboard usability or actual component behavior.
summary: The @utility Directive is one part of a predictable utility-first styling workflow.
Keep examples small, test the built interface and use version-matched documentation.
